Have you ever wondered what would happen if you tried to run the Boston Marathon in a business suit? Two friends, Paul Smith and Mike Spector, did just that in 1918. Paul, a native of Boston, owned a suit factory. Mike, a native of Baltimore, was a doctor of internal medicine. They were friends, and in 1918, Paul bet Mike he couldn’t run in a suit. Mike accepted the challenge, and they enlisted the help of the Fire Department to measure a course in Franklin Park Zoo, just a few miles from the starting line in Boston.
The two friends, along with 250 other men, donned suits and lined up at the starting line. Paul Smith, the favorite, had a good reason for his confidence. He had made the suit, which he was wearing, from his own special, lightweight, breathable fabric. The men took off, and the Fire Department measured a course of 2 ½ miles, which they ran a total of five times.
The winner, selected by a few seconds, was Mike Spector. Paul lost the $10 bet, and soon lost his title as well, when someone suggested the suit to him for a race. The current title holder is Sir Richard Branson, who won a similar race in 1986, and still holds the title 32 years later. Branson’s time was 22:29, and he beat out his friend, Stuart Ong, by 57 seconds.
What is the longest title for the world record for running a marathon while wearing a business suit, and who holds it?

Answer: The longest title for the world record for running a marathon (42.195km or 26.219 miles) while wearing a business suit is the Virgin Money London, and the current holder is Geoff "G" Atherton, who won the title in 2015. He was 35 years old when he set the record, and he beat the previous record by 34 minutes, with a time of 4:48:17. Geoff is a professional mountain biker.

In the two decades that have since passed, I haven't really seen any attempt to tie together all of these disparate themes, but I have noticed a few specific instances which, in various ways, stood out from one another. One of the more interesting examples from this topic was the book "Fight Club" by Chuck Palahniuk, which I'm aware had been discussed and reviewed many years ago, and I don't really have a lot to add to what has been said, but I can mention one or two things that I haven't seen emphasized as much. At the center of "Fight Club" is a character named Tyler Durden, who was the protagonist's dark side, but he was also a countercultural icon. Tyler's most vivid moment in the book is the "Project Mayhem" scene, where he leads his followers in a series of acts of vandalism and terrorism. What was their motivation? We are not told, but we can infer that it is to assert the will of Tyler, and to bring about some kind of societal change. Near the end, Tyler stands on the roof of a towering, abandoned building, addressing the protagonist as he did all along on the phone as "Mr.," and tells him to "be free like the wind." The "wind," of course, being the homeless, the down-and-out, the immigrants, and, in the xenophobic prelude, the "Project Mayhem" members of their kind with a last name that start with "W" (in "Fight Club", the names of Tyler's followers, all of them "W's," are often heard, such as "Brett, Jeff, Neil, and Bob"). In other words, Tyler wanted to liberate them from the yoke of the system, of the 9-to-5, of the rat race, of assignment, task, responsibility. In a word, he wanted to free them from work. This is a common sentiment, of course, but one that Tyler, of all people, was the last to tell. He loved the craft of manual work, and he derived great pleasure from it. He yearned to be a mechanic, a carpenter, or any kind of skilled laborer. He saw men as carpenters, and women as "choosers." His favorite woman was "The Assistant," and he both desired and hated her, for she was a living representation of the system that he despised. The Assistant represented the rules that Tyler wanted to overturn, and she represented the paper and ink that Tyler used to create his "recipes for disaster." She represented the "no smoking" signs he painted with red question marks, and the meetings with which she and her associates helped Tyler and his Project plan and execute. She was the moment when the pieces of the puzzle fell into place, the moment when Tyler's Project became a reality. She was the moment when the hammer broke the hand that grasped the dove. She was the idea that Project Mayhem was just a projection of chaos, and that true liberation was found in the freedom of the wind. The "wind," of course, was the unemployed. The characters in "Fight Club" were looking for a way to find meaning in their lives, and the only way to do so was through work. They were looking for a "club," a way to find a sense of belonging, and their lives were filled with purpose when they worked, when they created, when they destroyed. The "wind," the migrants, the unemployed, the rich, and their "club" were all brought together, and they were all united in Project Mayhem. The "club" was a secret society, and as such, it was a conspiracy. The conspiracy of the "club" was not just a personal one, but a philosophical movement, and the members of the "club" were something like the vanguard. The "wind" wanted to be free, and it did. It was free, and so it lived. It was free from the 9-to-5, and the rules, and the expectations, and the order, and the system, and the government, and the country, and the civilization, and the world, and God, and freedom. The "wind" was always free, but it was only recently that it understood that that was so. The "wind" was free when it left the factory, when it left the office, when it left school, and when it left the womb. The "wind" had always been free, but it had just misunderstood its own freedom. It had been told that it was enslaved, and had not argued the point, for it thought it had to fit in. The "wind" had to be told that it was free, and it had to be told to be that. "The Wind" was told this by Tyler, and so it left the factory, the office, the school, and the apartment, and it was told to, "Be free, for ever and ever, and make your own happiness." The "wind" was told to "live like the wind," and it did, and it still does, and it always will. This is why, to this day, the "wind" continues to live, and to be free. "Fight Club" was right, after all, and that means that the only reason the "system" had for existing is no longer there. The "wind" had asked, "What is the purpose of this thing we call life?" And the "system" had answered, "The production of consumers, the happy little business men, and their loved ones." The "wind" had rejected this, and Tyler had proposed an alternative: the "recruitment" of "free men," men who were "like the wind." Given an integer n, return true if it is a power of three. Otherwise, return false.
An integer n is a power of three, if there exists an integer x such that n == 3^x.

G. Tait, mention the work of the latter on wave theory, especially on the mechanical undulations proposed by Lord Kelvin. They also mention the work of Léon Foucault, especially the gyroscope, which he demonstrated a few months earlier. In the paper, Thomson and Tait refer to Léon Foucault's work with gyroscope, but they did not mention the details, but only that his demonstration has "a wider significance" and "is the origin of a long line of beautiful research." Foucault, in his paper, wrote that on 26th January 1851, he made a public demonstration at the Athenée in the Luxembourg, where he showed the absolute rotation of the earth by the deflection of the plane of a rapidly whirling horizontal glass paddle, 45 cm. Long, caused by the rotation of the earth. Léon Foucault was 34 years old at this time, and this was his second demonstration, for he showed the same phenomenon in October 1851, at the Salon, but this time he used a 12-meter spade, which made the demonstration much less clear, as in the previous, he had used a 4 and a half foot (2.44 m) had been sufficient to prove the rotation of the earth. In 1855, Léon Foucault obtained the patent for the gyroscope. The invention of the gyroscope was a major development, and it was used for various purposes, e.g. To measure the velocity of currents in the sea, for surveying, for navigation, for measuring the velocity of a ship, etc., and the gyroscope became essential for measuring the velocity of the ship. The gyroscope, however, did not reach its final form in the mid-50s, in 1858, in the exhibition of the French Academy, Foucault presented a survey of his work, and this was the first time, when he mentioned the effect of the earth's rotation on the velocity of the earth, but the publication was quickly overwhelmed by the general press, and Léon Foucault, the inventor of the gyroscope did not pay too much attention to the following fact: the scientists, when the audience, the judges, and the organizers stood up to ask questions, no one seemed to be interested in his work, but the small group of physicists, mathematicians, and geographers, when asked them, how would they solve the problem, gave quite different answers, some said that the effect of the earth's rotation could be measured with the proposed instruments, while the others stated that the effect was already known. As a matter of fact, when the same question was asked after the end of the presentation, the judges asked the following two questions: "President, have the honors?" and "Can the two lecturers give us the course?" The audience then dispersed without paying any attention to the work of Foucault. The reason for this is not mentioned in the available documents, but since the questions asked, it is obvious that there was a strong tension between those who opposed the research of Foucault, and the supporters of his work. The main argument of Léon Foucault was that the possible applications of the gyroscope are not in navigation, but in physics, and the gyroscope is a tool to measure the earth's rotation. The measurement, however, required a pendulum, and Foucault used a 7.5 meter long one, which was twice as long as the one he used in his previous demonstration. The reason he applied a longer pendulum was to increase the sensitivity of the instrument, in order to measure the effect of the earth's rotation more precisely. If the length of the pendulum is fixed, the sensitivity of the measurement still depended on the length, and Foucault noticed that the longer the pendulum, the more sensitive the measurement was. He could increase the length of the pendulum, hoping that the result will be even more precise, but since the maximum length of a material pendulum is limited, Foucault needed a way to increase the sensitivity of the measurement even more than two times, and this was achieved by using a secondary pendulum, the same one used by Foucaault, but much longer. If the length of the pendulum is fixed, the measurement results were good, but not sufficient to provide a high level of precision. If the length of the pendulum was the limiting factor in the measurement sensitivity, Foucault called it in vain. However, if the length of the pendulum allowed a certain range, then the measurement could be accurate, and in order to increase the sensitivity even further, Foucault introduced the term "long pendulum" and this was the only new thing. The length of the pendulum was not limited, but in order to get a measurable difference, a second, longer pendulum was need, and this was done. The length of the longer pendulum was about 15 meters, but the exact length was not so important, the only thing important was, that the length had to be at least 15 meters. It is curious to know, that Léö Foucaau made the following miscalculation: he wrote that for a pendulum of 7.5 meters, the error measured is 11 centimeters, and the value of π is 10. The correction depended on the state of the instrument, and many other factors, and the researchers had to correct the measurement made in a certain time, and this correction was necessary to obtain the correct measurement, and it took some time to do it. One astronomer, when the experiment was in progress to measure the velocity of the earth, stated that the measurement is not correct. The other scientists in the audience quickly rejected the correction, and disagreed with their colleague. This was the reason for a funny retort from Foucault, when he said: "The honor of the astronomers consists in not making such mistakes." This was a witty reply, but a completely wrong one, as the researchers involved were physicists, not astronomers. This was a remarkable reply, and ended the discussion, and the comedy. Foucault also published a memoir, in which the mistake was only mentioned.

In the text we can see that Foucault claimed that the angle between the plane of the pendulum and the vertical (11 degrees) was too small, and the length of the pendulum (15 meters) is too short. He also claimed that the air had a considerable influence on the pendulum, and this opposed the generally accepted fact, that the air has no significant effect on the pendulum.

Léon Foucault, in his first experiment, used a 7.4 meter long pendulum, and this was the second longest pendulum in history. The longest one, 22.3 meters long, was built by Franz Xaver von Zach, an Austrian astronomer, who, together with other scientists, was also watching the experiment. The difference between the results of the two experiments was so small, that Zach did not want to accept the result, and he built a pendulum with 22.3 meters, the longest in the world, and with this he found a different result.

Foucault's and Zach's experiments were not the first, as the scientists repeated the experiment with the torsion pendulum in a more careful way, and with many improvements, but without detecting the effect. The reason that Foucaault did not see the effect was that he made the measurements at the wrong time, when the influence of the earth's rotation, being so, had already gone, and the air had already canceled the effect of the rotation. If the pendulum was not deflected, and the measurements were already made, then the influence of the earth's rotation was not observable, and the experiments seemed to have contradicted the theoretical prediction. Several attempts were made to improve the instruments, and to make the measurements in a better way, but all of them failed to detect the effect of the rotation of the earth on the plane of the pendulum. The reason for this was, that the instruments used were not sensitive enough. If the instruments were improved, and if the measurements were done in a more precise way, then the effect of the rotation of the earth could be detected, and the temperature and the air had no influence. So if the measurement was precise enough, then the experiments of Foucaault and Zach would also give the same results.

In 1862, Léon Foucault made an experiment, using the same apparatus as Zach, a 22.3 meter long pendulum, and this was the most precise experiment made. The pendulum was in the observatory of the church of Saint Pierre, and Foucault measured the angle of the deflection for four hours, with a precision of 1/10,000 of a degree, and he found the value 11.3 degrees, which is 0.1 degree higher than the value obtained by Zach. The four poems above (by T.S. Eliot and by an unpublished, anonymous author) express a common theme: a search for the meaning of life. At the time of their publication, this theme may have been familiar to many. As the 20th-century is filled with writers, each in their own unique perspective on life and the struggle for meaning, the years of their composition saw a rich and ongoing exploration of this theme. Some of these poems became famous, and continue to be read today. What follows is the appreciation of these poems, but not their fame, which has made them almost a cliché, and therefore, obscured their artistic value. Rather than compare and criticize, I would like to simply remember them as masterpieces.

The beauty of "The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock" and "Four Quartets" by T.S. Eliot is well beyond the reach of most art. The power of their words is such that one never thinks of them as being the product of a particular time in history. They sound like the essence of the human condition. In the nearly one thousand pages of the "The Complete Prose of T.S. Eliot" (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2014), edited by Eliot’s heirs, we find a different quality in his prose. The critical essays are often reductive, and can be contentious, but either way, they are of little interest in themselves. What is significant about them is the way they are arranged, the way they demonstrate Eliot’s mind in the process of forming his own aesthetic.

Eliot was a writer of the 20th century, and his work—poetry as well as criticism—is rooted in the intellectual and artistic history of his own age. His most innovative works, especially the verse, are famous, and, to a considerable extent, admired. But then there is another side of Eliot, a lesser-known side, the side of the popularizer, the side that for years wrote introduction after introduction for other authors, a practice that has sometimes produced resentment. One can hardly blame readers for finding the critical essays of a living writer tedious, and for eagerly turning to the work of more promising youth. But in this case, one must question the precedent that underlies a living writer’s body of critical prose. The essays are a kind of record, and in Eliot’s case, they represent a lifelong commitment to a particular mode of literary and cultural criticism. To put it differently: an 1,100-page anthology of critical prose, assemblance or patchwork, at a rate of 10 pages a day, will take just under a year to read. What better way, then, to end a lifetime devoted to criticism than with the publication of such a complete collection? And yet, had Eliot paused at 300, 500, 700, or 800 pages, he would have been able to prepare a final, more concise, and better-edited selection of his critical prose for posterity. So what motivates a writer to publish, in the form of an anthology, a complete collection of his critical prose, a work that represents no final, distilled, or definitive statement, but rather an accumulation of his work, warts and all, over the course of a lifetime? The answer is that Eliot’s complete prose, with all its revisions and corrections, is a monumental work in its own right. In fact, it is a major work of criticism, and one that, like his verse, is a testament to Eliot’s formidable mind.

Paper: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and a decoder. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the best models from the literature. We show that the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data.

We present a state-of-the-art speech recognition system developed using end-to-end deep learning. Our architecture is significantly simpler than traditional speech systems, which rely on laboriously engineered processing pipelines; these traditional systems also tend to perform poorly when used in noisy environments. In contrast, our system does not need hand-designed components to model background noise, reverberation, or speaker variation, but instead directly learns a function that is robust to such effects. We do not need a phoneme dictionary, nor even the concept of a "phoneme." Key to our approach is a well-optimized RNN training system that uses multiple GPUs, as well as a set of novel data synthesis techniques that allow us to efficiently obtain a large amount of varied data for training. Our system, called Deep Speech, outperforms previously published results on the widely studied Switchboard Hub5'00, achieving 16.0% error on the full test set. Deep Speech also handles challenging noisy environments better than widely used, state-of-the-art commercial speech systems.Collapse

instruction:
Create a short, concise summary of the paper based on its abstract.

Few-shot learning (FSL) is one of the key future steps in machine learning and raises a lot of attention. In this paper, we focus on the FSL problem of dialogue understanding, which contains two closely related tasks: intent detection and slot filling. Dialogue understanding has been proven to benefit a lot from jointly learning the two sub-tasks. However, such joint learning becomes challenging in the few-shot scenarios: on the one hand, the sparsity of samples greatly magnifies the difficulty of modeling the connection between the two tasks; on the other hand, how to jointly learn multiple tasks in the few-shot setting is still less investigated. In response to this, we introduce FewJoint, the first FSL benchmark for joint dialogue understanding. FewJoint provides a new corpus with 59 different dialogue domains from real industrial API and a code platform to ease FSL experiment set-up, which are expected to advance the research of this field. Further, we find that insufficient performance of the few-shot setting often leads to noisy sharing between two sub-task and disturbs joint learning. To tackle this, we guide slot with explicit intent information and propose a novel trust gating mechanism that blocks low-confidence intent information to ensure high quality sharing. Besides, we introduce a Reptile-based meta-learning strategy to achieve better generalization in unseen few-shot domains. In the experiments, the proposed method brings significant improvements on two datasets and achieve new state-of-the-art performance.

I am a Hungarian, and as I'm writing this, the year 2021 is not yet over. The year 2020, August, a wave of the coronavirus hit the world, sending many countries backwards by a couple of years in public health, and by one in civil and data science. As the pandemic reached its bottom half, some experts kept warning of a second, even third or fourth possible virus wave in the autumn. The majority of the world's population listened to them, but not many paid too much attention. They were right, of course, to be worried, but they were too optimistic about the autumn. As it turned out, the world still had plenty of virus in stock, and a new wave was not needed to bring the daily number of cases to a new record. All that was needed was a little relaxation, a slight lifting of restrictions.

In Hungary, as a result, the number of daily cases spiked, far more than during the first wave, and the number of the seriously ill has exceeded the capacity of the hospitals. The country is now in a deep lockdown, similar to the one a year ago, but this one is much stricter. The main difference is that while the earlier one was a "light" one, the current one is "heavy". The government and the experts are both aware of this, and they are both responsible for it. The former because they decided to impose a lockdown, the latter because they warned of its consequences.

If the experts were right, and the lockdown was necessary, then why did they not emphasize it more a year ago, when they first announced it? They could have saved many lives. The answer is simple: a lockdown of this kind was not an option, because the number of cases was already out of control. It was not possible to spring a surprise like this with a week's notice, and a more extended preparation would have made no difference, because the cases were already piling up in hospitals, and many people were dying. If the experts had realized the situation earlier, they would have, so the argument goes, acted earlier. This, though, is not true. At the time, the healthcare sector was already overwhelmed, and the experts were right in not ordering a lockdown then. If they had acted earlier, the result would have been the same, but with a milder virus wave.

The experts, and the government, were caught off guard by the magnitude of the crisis. They were not sure, and still are not, of what to do, or how to handle the situation. This is the best they can do, and they are doing it well. If the experts had been better prepared, and if they had not been caught off guard, the number of cases and the death toll could have been reduced. But this would have required a different, more informed and educated approach to the virus, and to the measures taken against it. It would have required a different leadership, one that is not afraid of taking the risk of not following the herd, and one that is not afraid of making decisions, even unpopular ones, and standing by them, and learning from their consequences. But this is a lot to ask. What we have are experts, and a leadership, and both will probably do what they can, which is not much, and make mistakes, which is human, and hope for the best, which is all we can do in a difficult and unpredictable situation.

This is not an easy time to be a leader, an expert, or an ordinary person. It is a test, a big one, and we are all, to some extent, failing it. But the good news is that the worst is probably already behind us, and that there is light at the end of the tunnel. If we keep wearing our masks, maintaining distance, and if we get vaccinated, we will overcome this, and we will emerge from the crisis stronger, more united, and more grateful for the things we once took for granted. The next year will not be easy, but it will be better. 2022 will be even better, and the years after that will be the best. We will not forget this year, but we will remember it as the year we won the battle against the virus, and as the first year of the next period, the period of recovery.

1 avocado

1 Tbsp Dijon mustard

2 Tbsp red onion, chopped
2 green onions, chopped
1 Tbsp fresh cilantro, chopped

On February 14th, 1842, the poet John Keats died, in Rome, at the age of 25, after a long and painful battle with tuberculosis. In a letter of 3rd December 1840, he wrote: “I have many time wished for absolute power, that I might make Britain (and Italy) and every land and every sea as free as the spirit of a man from slavery.”

Here’s a poem that I have composed a while ago, to honor the memory of Keats, and a few other things:

And the winds, they blow the songs
Of heroes gone before
Across the years, and oceans
To lift the souls of others

Through the ages, like a hero’s cry
Resounds a sound
The echo of a valorous “Adieu!”
Of those who, for the world, have died

Their songs, their lives, their cries
Their tears, their hopes, their dreams
Their bonds, their faith, their loves
Their struggles, their wars, their schemes

All these, the price of time
And yet, an echo of their choosing
Lingers, and calls mankind
To rise, and find their being

For freedom.

Based on the passage above, the works "Ode on a Grecian Urn" and "To His Final Martin" by John Keats can both be categorized into the following:

1. Works written by John Keats
2. Works that talk about death

Passage: “I have many time wished for absolute power, that I might make Britain (and Italy) and every land and every sea as free as the spirit of a man from slavery.”

Through the “Ode on a Grecian Urn,” John Keats laments about the tyranny of time, and the inability to stop it. In “To His Final Martin,” however, the poem is not death per se, but the wish for it, as an escape from the prison of a consumptive’s body. Keats ponders on the desire for absolute power, to free not just Britain and Italy, but every land and sea, to mirror the freedom of the human spirit. These two works can, thus, be related to the themes of death and freedom, as they are products of Keats’ understanding and yearning to break free from the shackles of death and time.

2. Ode on a Grecian Urn and Bright Star

The title “Bright Star” is sometimes affiliated with “To the Nightingale,” but its real reference is to John Keats’ poem, “Bright Star! Would I were stept / In death, the pastaries of your realm, / Or sickened by your dewy fear, / Fall on, as I fall sleep! / No, no, go not to Lethe, neither twist, / Wolf, in the ancient fane; / For I must die, and all the while / This is, and so, and so, / grows old and calm, draws out / Long and larger, yet unroll’d, / The lofty Nature to enthrone, / And the dull world hereby know, / That in thy beauty’s height, / Time in Eternity invests; / And, for this, be dear dead things, / The frozen-out, the stiff twins, / Soft star, be nothing else but noiseless, / Eternally quiet, and immortal; / No, no, go not to Lethe, no, you shall not go.”

“Bright Star!” is a prayer to the star for a peaceful death, a wish to be in the star’s realm of immortality, as a step into death. The poem, however, is not a lamentation of death, but a tribute to the beauty of the star, which is the same theme as in “Ode on a Grecian Urn.” In both works, Keats laments the inability to halt the passing of time, and the need to find eternity. The urn represents a form of eternity, which Keats confers to the “Bright Star” as well, for it is “unroll’d, / The lofty Nature to enthrone, / And the dull world hereby know, / That in thy beauty’s height, / Time in Eternity invests.”

3. Ode to a Nightingale and To Autumn

“Ode to a Nightingale” is a poem about the poet’s desire to escape from the burden of time, and “To Autumn” is a tribute to the season of autumn, for its ability to slow down time. In “Ode to a Nightingale,” Keats laments the passage of time, which brings with it the loss of innocence and the onset of experience, a time when “the chill derision sits / In a cloud, in a rift of blue ice, / And the lonely spirit fails, / Forsaken, unassailed.” He longs to escape from this time, and to dwell with the “Nightingale” in a world where time stops. In “To Autumn,” however, the theme is not the desire to escape from time, but the ability of autumn to slow down time. Autumn is a season of death, decay, and harvest, and in this poem, Keats presents the season as a goddess, and describes the events that take place under its reign. The season slows down the world, and “matures the vine, and the unskillful vintager toil / And make groan the full seas, and the woods / And, though the whole world turn to leaf, / Mingles the love of life with the light of the setting sun.”

4. Ode to a Grecian Urn and The Epic of Gilgamesh

The resemblance of “Ode to a Grecian Urn” and the epic of Gilgamesh lies in the former’s implicit acknowledgment of man’s inevitable journey into death, and the latter’s explicit exposition of the theme. Both the epic, and “Ode to a Grecian Urn” are a story of the human struggle against the transience of life, and the search for some form of immortality. The epic, however, is more forthright, as it narrates the story of King Gilgamesh, his fear of death, and his quest for immortality, which leads him to the discovery of the secret of the “Sumerian” afterlife, and his conclusion that “tomorrow, I shall join her (Mami).” The “Ode to a Grecian Urn,” on the other hand, depicts in its visual imagery, the eternal objects in the urn’s reliefs, and the transitory, stricken away, the result of time’s progress, suggesting that the fear of death is overcome by the joy of immortality.

The article God of War 4 for PlayStation (and its predecessor, PlayStation 2's God of War 2, both of them, here God of War 1 and God of War 4, are available for free play on their respective demo discs on PlayStation 5's demo mode) is not new. Its lore, its story, and its characters, they all have been analyzed, discussed, and overanalyzed. The two discs, God of War 1 and God of War 4, take Kratos, the God Killer, on a swashbuckler adventure in Hades and other places. In the course of this, Kratos, the living embodiment of the human soul's end, meets various characters, and spins their tales. At the end of the game, with all the characters alive, and the world in its beginning-of-times, all is well – or as well as it can be in a world, where the sun stops in the sky, and the dead rise. The end of the game is a perfect end, and, as such, not true to the series' tradition. Yes, it was a tradition, but it was a stupid one. A proper game.

The game, as the old, as the new

I still remember the first time I played a God of War game. I played it in search of something, I think I was searching for entertainment, and I got it. But the God of War series is not a game about endless fun and entertainment, no, it is a game about the horror of human condition. And it is a powerful example to help you understand the horror of human condition, and it works much more effectively than, say, Uncharted 4: A Thief's End, a game which is also a great example, but in a different degree. While Uncharted 4 conveys the horror of human condition in a very, very distant way, God of War conveys it in an immediate, visceral, and up-close fashion. To understand this, let's compare these two games, and, as I will do so, I won't be requiring too much from the reader, as this is common knowledge, and can be experienced in the games.

Both of them deal with death. While the God of War series, from the very beginning, has been dealing with death, Uncharted 4: A Thief's End, made the subject of one of its central elements. However, while the God of War treated death as a part of reality, Uncharted 4 approached it as a concept. The God of War shows death as a part of life, and something that is real, and something that the player had to experience in order to progress in the game. Uncharted 4, on the other hand, puts in question the very nature of death, and forces the player to think about it, and whether it is, in fact, a reality, or just an illusion. But, as I am not a philosopher, I will not ponder the nature of death and its reality, but will focus on the two deaths.

In the God of War series, death is not a new element, and, as the story of the series progresses, it becomes a bigger, and more important part of it. Kratos, the protagonist, is a God, who, in his first appearance, is in the process of becoming, as he is still an anguished human soul. He is neither exactly justifiable, nor excusable, but his actions are not entirely illogical, and he is not entirely without reason. As the story progresses, and Kratos' personality changes, he becomes more and more ruthless, and his actions are more and more heinous, but, as a player, we still have no reason to object to his actions, as he is a God, and his new, more ruthless personality is something that the player comes to accept. In God of War 3, the story puts the main character, Kratos, in a difficult situation, as he is the only one who can stop the three, giant, titantic Horsemen, from opening the gates of Elysium, and, once opened, release a wave of power that will grant immortality to all the fallen heroes, and, as a result, end the natural order of life and death. Kratos, in this situation, takes it upon himself to stop them, and sets off on a quest to hunt them down, and kill them. This, his ultimate mission, is something the player fully supports, and, as a result, Kratos fights them, defeating them in a long, and grueling, but spectacular, battle. It is only then, after the defeat of the Horsemen, that Kratos, in a state of shock, and, afterwards, finds himself in a situation where he is forced to make a difficult decision, a decision that will, in the end, cost him everything, as he is forced to sacrifice everything he has ever wanted, and, in doing so, undo all that he has done, and, as a result, restore the natural order of life and death.

Uncharted 4: A Thief's End, on the other hand, also deals with death, but in a different way. Nathan Drake, the protagonist, is a treasure hunter, and a man of action, but, at the same time, a writer, who records the stories that he comes across. instruction: What factors would you consider when designing an inclusive and accessible public transportation system?
output:
1. Multiple means: Design public transportation with various options to meet the needs of a diverse population, including:

a. People with disabilities: Plan and design for public transportation services that meet the needs of people with different disabilities, such as visual, physical, hearing, and more.

b. Accessibility: Ensure that public transportation services are designed to be as accessible as possible, using a variety of the various tools and measures described below.

2. Accessibility: Make public transportation, as used in a society or population with people of all age, one of the key element of public transportation accessibility in order to promote public transportation as a service. In this case, accessibility is often a key factor, and planning public transportation as such can help.

3. Consideration: Be aware of the importance of accessibility in public transportation systems. Accessibility may not be the only factor to consider, but understanding the need is important. Raise awareness on the importance of accessibility to facilitate cooperation between all stakeholders.

4. Raise awareness: Encourage and support an pro-accessibility culture, both in general and in the context of public transportation.

5. Train the relevant people: The people responsible for the accessibility of public transportation services in their area or region may need to be trained to follow best practices. Provide training on new skills, and maintain an awareness of any new developments in the topic of accessibility in public transportation.

6. Plan ahead: In general, to ensure an accessible public transportation system, it is a good practice to plan early. Designing the public transportation system, policies, and practices of a region through an integrated and collaborative approach, in all, requires time as a key factor.

7. Review existing approaches: Once you are planning public transportation, whether new designs or optimizations, understanding the current practice, practices, and standards of other similar products is important to gauge the level of accessibility.

8. Implement: Once you have a clear understanding of what an accessible public transportation system is, introduce and implement policies that support the same are called for. Relevant newspapers:

Title: Google to mark quantum computing milestone with Schrödinger parodies

The New York Times article "Science Ask: What Is a Cat?" reported the reasons, but not the selected evidence, while the UK Guardian article prepared a "punch" from the latter, and relied on the following evidence. The week before both publications, the only reference to quantum cats in The Times was a book review (in the twice reviewed form — by the author and by Tom Levenson, with the latter being more focused on style). The author of the review, Brian Clegg, also wrote a non-review article, in which he discussed the content of the book, but the main emphasis was on the possibility to present the ideas in the book's pages and, well, on the power, actually, the ability, that quantum physics can offer to a person determined enough to dig deep and make some effort, but also to explain. The reviewed book (Chaos, Elegance, and Evolution by George B. Dyson. Basic Books, 2018, 320 pages) is by George B. Dyson, and in a sense, three books in one: a book about George, a book about quantum physics, and a book about George. About the style, the book is long, but it is a narrative, and the title correctly describes its content. Let me see then why the New York Times and The Guardian written on the topic, the former more broadly than the latter, chose their topics.

In the first part of the book, Dyson tells (among other things) his personal story, which, as it happens, is a story of a rather determined person. He read and thought a great deal, and, as a result, he had some original (some of the ideas, not unique, but rather interesting) insights into his 40s, say. One part of the book, though, is the author's attempt (however difficult and time-consuming) to do some advanced science, and it is, obviously, in the field of quantum physics (and, more specifically, in the subfield, relevant to the recent developments, of quantum computing). This is, of course, a fair amount of the book, but not the book itself. The part that is relevant to quantum computing and takes a significant share in the book is the author's attempt to explain the science he does, and this part, being a result of dilligence, is, well, a result of the effort to explain, but, unfortunately, this part is not a suitable place, in its current form, even for the attempt, as the book lacks the necessary space. This part is, as it should, accompanied by a lot of references, but the references are in the form of footnotes, and it is a pity that they are so. It would be more useful if the references were the main text. To some extent, the footnotes, extensive as they are, give the impression of a paper, and since they are footnotes, they could have been moved to the book, but still, a paper inside a book is no true substitute for a real reference at the end, and, of course, finding a reference in the middle of a paragraph is not the same as in a footnote, and, on the other hand, the absence of a footnote is not the same as a reference in the main text. The footnotes, in other words, although extensive, cannot replace real references, and, consequently, a paper, even if it is embedded in the book, is no substitute for the real, final, references. This, unfortunately, results in the fact that the main part, although the most effort-demanding (and, thus, interesting) one, will be, because of its length, inaccessible for its most valuable part, and the part of the book, which is, at the same time, easy to read, will be, because of its conciseness, a bit unexplained.

There is only one reference in the book that I would like to note, except for the above one, which I have already mentioned. It is not a reference, but the title itself: the book's title, Chaos, Elegance, and Evolution, is (short) the thesis that the search for, and the understanding of, the fundamental principles of the physical world, has led, and will lead, to a better understanding of the world, and, probably, of evolution. This is, of course, a very brief and general statement, but in this particular form, a correct one, and, I believe, the most appropriate one that could be made, generally and correctly, out of the context of the book.

George B. Dyson, Chaos, Elegance, and Evolution. Basic Books, 2018, 320 pages. ISBN: 9781549113269.

There are a few books of the quantum theme that I follow, and I have read all of them, with varying degrees of interest. This is a book I would recommend. The author is an amateur, a self-proclaimed "amateur," which, in this context, is a praise. The book is not about physics, but about the people, the ideas, the culture, the scientists, and the technology, and it is, above all, a love letter, paid to a field that the author loves, and, in a way, he is not wrong to do so. The author does not offer a lot of new insights, but he does not claim to. What he does claim to do, he does: to explain, to entertain, to write. The book is not too long, and the footnotes make it even shorter, which, in this case, is a good thing. The book, Chaos, Elegance, and Evolution, is a pleasant read, and I would recommend it to anyone who is interested in the history of quantum physics, but not the theory as it is, but its discovery. This could be of particular interest to computer scientists, as quantum computing is a natural development of this field, and the first ideas and the first steps in this area are part of the history of quantum physics. The book, in this respect, is a good read, but, then again, this is the only part of the history of quantum physics that I find interesting, so I would be driven to read only this part, should it be a textbook. The author, George B. Dyson, is to be commended for writing this book, and I, for one, would be looking forward to his next book, if he were to write one, but, then again, this is George B. Dyson, and this is exactly what he has already written: a book.

This is a book I would recommend to my students, but not as a textbook, as it is not one. As a reference, it is not a textbook, either, as more than 2/3 of its pages cover the material I would like to see in the first half. It is a good book, but, then again, its scope is much wider than the one of a textbook. This is not a book about quantum mechanics, but about the physicists who made this subject, and it is, at the same time, a book about the engineers who turned the developments in quantum physics into practical applications. The book is not about quantum theory, but about the people who created it, and about the devices that were built using the ideas. This, again, is a book about the history of quantum physics, but a history that is very personal, and, as such, it is a story about people, their ideas, and their contributions. This is not a book about the principles of quantum mechanics, but about the people who made these principles, and the technology that these principles made possible. This is a book I would like to have on my bookshelf, not next to my textbooks, but next to my other copies of history books. It is a book I would keep for ready reference, but about what? Not about a textbook, and not about a reference, but about a leisure read. I read this book with pleasure, and I would probably read it again with pleasure, but, while I read it, I would not think of keeping it as a textbook, a reference, or even for ready reference. I would think of it as a book, and a very good one, at that.

The author, George B. Dyson, is an amateur, and, as such, a good writer. The book is well written, and the style is easy to read, the sentences short, the structure simple, and the footnotes numerous, but not excessive. The book is a pleasure to read, and I would recommend it, but not as a textbook (which it is not) or even for ready reference (it is in a form suitable for reading), but, simply, as a book. If you are looking for a textbook, you would find this one interesting, as a textbook, but only if you are already familiar with the subject. If you are looking for a reference, this one is good, but only for ready reference, and, again, only if you are already familiar with the subject. If you want to read it, you will not need a copy, as you can find a copy, but you will need the book, and this is, finally, one you should buy, not borrow, or download, but read. You will not do
